# Overview

## Background

The political turbulence in the United States of America has made global trade one of the most closely watched topics in recent years. Their actions and policies greatly affect the world's economy and individual countries want to know what impact they will have on their own economies. This assignment examines Singapore's trade data to gain insights on their economic relationships with other nations.

## Objectives

The goal of this assignment is to critically analyze visualizations from Singapore's trade report and improve them using `ggplot2` and other relevant R packages. The makeover should enhance clarity, readability, and interpretability while ensuring that key trade insights are effectively communicated.

# Getting Started

## Installing and loading packages

The following R packages will be used:

-   **tidyverse:** A collection of R packages designed for data manipulation, exploration, and visualization, providing a consistent and easy-to-use syntax.

-   **plotly**: R package for creating interactive and dynamic data visualizations.

-   **ggthemes:** Offers additional themes and color schemes for ggplot2, enabling more visually appealing and customized plots.

-   **knitr:** An R package designed for dynamic report generation. It integrates R code with documents to produce well-formatted reports, tables, and visualizations.

-   **scales:** Allows customization of axis labels, breaks, and scales in ggplot2, improving plot readability and presentation.

-   **tsibble:** Provides a framework for working with time-series data in a tidy format.

-   **lubridate:** Helps parse, manipulate, and analyze date/time information.

-   **feasts**: Works with tsibble to analyze time-series components (trend, seasonality, residuals).

-   **readxl:** An R package for reading Excel files (.xls and .xlsx) into R.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(readxl, tidyverse, plotly, ggthemes, knitr, scales, tsibble, lubridate, feasts)
```

# The Datasets

The data used are from the Department of Statistics Singapore [website](https://www.singstat.gov.sg/find-data/search-by-theme/trade-and-investment/merchandise-trade/latest-data). Specifically, we will be importing the following excel spreadsheets:

-   Merchandise Trade By Commodity Section, (At Current Prices), Monthly \[TradeCommodity.xlsx T1\]

-   Merchandise Trade By Region and Selected Market (Imports), Monthly \[TradeRegion.xlsx T1\]

-   Merchandise Trade By Region and Selected Market (Domestic Exports), Monthly \[TradeRegion.xlsx T2\]

-   Merchandise Trade By Region and Selected Market (Re-Exports), Monthly \[TradeRegion.xlsx T3\]

## Importing the Data

```{r}
df1 <- read_excel("data/TradeCommodity.xlsx", sheet = 'T1')
```

The columns for TradeCommodity.xlsx was shown to have a mix of numeric and character types. Therefore, col_types = "text" is used to standardised the column type to text.

```{r}
df1 <- read_excel("data/TradeCommodity.xlsx", sheet = 'T1', col_types = "text")
df2 <- read_excel("data/TradeRegion.xlsx", sheet = 'T1')
df3 <- read_excel("data/TradeRegion.xlsx", sheet = 'T2')
df4 <- read_excel("data/TradeRegion.xlsx", sheet = 'T3')
df5 <- read_excel("data/TradeCommodity_Mod.xlsx", sheet = 'T1', col_types = "text")
```

## V1 Data Preparation

First, we examine the data to confirm the structure. We will need to convert the column names (Year-Month) into rows.

```{r}
head(df1)
```

### Check for missing values

Even though colSums(is.na(df1)) shows no missing values, we can observe that there are indeed 'na' character strings in the data. However, they are only observed in the data before 1975. This would not affect the assignment as we are only concerned about the data starting from 2020-2024.

```{r}
colSums(is.na(df1))
```

### Reshape the Data Using pivot_longer()

```{r}
colnames(df1) <- as.character(colnames(df1))

commodity <- df1 %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`, names_to = "Year_Month", values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Trade_Value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Trade_Value))) 
```

### Filter out the relevant data

For the first visualisation, we are specifically concerned about the Total Merchandise Imports (At Current Prices), Total Merchandise Exports (At Current Prices) and the Total Merchandise Trade (Imports + Exports), (At Current Prices) from 2020 to 2024. Therefore, we filter those rows out.

```{r}
commodity_total <- commodity %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% c("Total Merchandise Imports, (At Current Prices)", "Total Merchandise Exports, (At Current Prices)", "Total Merchandise Trade, (At Current Prices)"))
```

```{r}
commodity_total <- commodity_total %>%
  mutate(Year = year(parse_date_time(Year_Month, orders = "ym"))) %>% 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2024) %>%
  group_by(Year, `Data Series`) %>%
  summarise(Total_Trade_Value = sum(Trade_Value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()
```

### Final Look at the Datasets

```{r}
kable(head(commodity_total))
commodity_total
```

## V2 Data Preparation

### Check for missing values

We can see there are no missing values in all 3 datasets.

```{r}
colSums(is.na(df2))
colSums(is.na(df3))
colSums(is.na(df4))
```

### Reshape and Filter Only for 2024 and Selected Countries

For the second visualisation, we are specifically concerned about the imports, exports and total trade volume with China, Malaysia, United States of America, Taiwan, Europe, Indonesia, Hong Kong, Republic of Korea, Japan, and Thailand in 2024. Therefore, we filter those rows out. We also combine domestic exports and re-exports into just exports with bind_rows().

```{r}
target_countries <- c("China", "Malaysia", "United States", 
                      "Taiwan", "Europe", "Indonesia", "Hong Kong", 
                      "Korea, Rep Of", "Japan", "Thailand")
```

```{r}
imports <- df2 %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  filter(startsWith(Date, "2024")) %>%
  mutate(Trade_Type = "Imports") 

domestic_ex <- df3 %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  filter(startsWith(Date, "2024")) %>%
  mutate(Trade_Type = "Exports") 

re_ex <- df4 %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  filter(startsWith(Date, "2024")) %>%
  mutate(Trade_Type = "Exports") 

exports <- bind_rows(domestic_ex, re_ex)

```

### Combine both dataframes

```{r}
combined_trade <- bind_rows(imports, exports)
```

### Summarize Trade Value for the Whole Year of 2024

```{r}
annual_trade <- combined_trade %>%
  group_by(`Data Series`, Trade_Type) %>%
  summarise(Trade_Value = sum(Trade_Value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

### Final look

```{r}
kable(head(annual_trade))
annual_trade
```

## V3 Data Preparation

We will be using a modified version of TradeCommodity.xlsx. This dataset contains proper labelling for imports and exports. For example, Machinery & Transport Equipment is renamed to Machinery & Transport Equipment \[Imports\] and Machinery & Transport Equipment \[Exports\] where necessary.

### Reshape the Data Using pivot_longer()

```{r}
colnames(df5) <- as.character(colnames(df5))

commodity_mod <- df5 %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`, names_to = "Year_Month", values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Trade_Value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Trade_Value))) 
```

### Filter out the relevant data

We will be filtering out the following commodity categories, both imports and exports, in 2024: Machinery & Transport Equipment, Chemicals & Chemical Products, Miscellaneous Manufactured Articles, Manufactured Goods, Food & Live Animals, Animal & Vegetable Oils Beverages & Tobacco, Crude Materials and other Miscellaneous Items.

```{r}
commodity_category <- commodity_mod %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% c("Food & Live Animals [Imports]", "Beverages & Tobacco [Imports]", "Crude Materials (Excl Fuels) [Imports]", "Animal & Vegetable Oils Fats & Waxes [Imports]", "Chemicals & Chemical Products [Imports]", "Manufactured Goods [Imports]", "Machinery & Transport Equipment [Imports]", "Miscellaneous Manufactured Articles [Imports]", "Miscellaneous (Excluding Oil Bunkers) [Imports]", "Food & Live Animals [Exports]", "Beverages & Tobacco [Exports]", "Crude Materials (Excl Fuels) [Exports]", "Animal & Vegetable Oils Fats & Waxes [Exports]", "Chemicals & Chemical Products [Exports]", "Manufactured Goods [Exports]", "Machinery & Transport Equipment [Exports]", "Miscellaneous Manufactured Articles [Exports]", "Miscellaneous (Excluding Oil Bunkers) [Exports]"))
```

```{r}
commodity_category <- commodity_category %>%
  mutate(Year = year(parse_date_time(Year_Month, orders = "ym"))) %>% 
  filter(Year == 2024) %>%
  group_by(Year, `Data Series`) %>%
  summarise(Total_Trade_Value = sum(Trade_Value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()
```

### Separate into 'Commodity' and 'Trade_Type'

```{r}
commodity_category <- commodity_category %>%
  separate(`Data Series`, into = c("Commodity", "Trade_Type"), sep = " \\[", remove = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(Trade_Type = gsub("\\]", "", Trade_Type))
```

### Final Look at the Datasets

```{r}
kable(head(commodity_category))
commodity_category
```

## V4 Data Preparation

### Time Series Visualisation

For time series visualisation, the same dataset from V2 will be used, except we will be filtering from 2015 to 2024 and keeping the datasets separate (imports, domestic exports, re-exports).

```{r}

imports_v4 <- df2 %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Date = ym(Date)) %>%  
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)

domestic_ex_v4 <- df3 %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Date = ym(Date)) %>%  
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)

re_ex_v4 <- df3 %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Date = ym(Date)) %>%  
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)
  

```

### Time Series Analysis

For Time Series Analysis, we will need to transpose the dataset and convert the tibble dataset to tsibble.

#### Transpose and Filter

```{r}
import1 <- as.data.frame(t(df2))
dom_ex1 <- as.data.frame(t(df3))
re_ex1 <- as.data.frame(t(df4))

colnames(import1) <- import1[1, ]
colnames(dom_ex1) <- dom_ex1[1, ]
colnames(re_ex1) <- re_ex1[1, ]

import_tp <- import1[-1, ]
dom_ex_tp <- dom_ex1[-1, ]
re_ex_tp <- re_ex1[-1, ]

import_tp <- import_tp %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "Date") %>%
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date),   
         Date = ym(Date)) %>%         
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)  

dom_ex_tp <- dom_ex_tp %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "Date") %>%
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date), 
         Date = ym(Date)) %>%
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)

re_ex_tp <- re_ex_tp %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "Date") %>%
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date), 
         Date = ym(Date)) %>%
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)
```

#### Convert to tsibble

```{r}
import_tsibble <- import_tp %>%
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(Date)) %>%
  as_tsibble(index = `Month`)

dom_ex_tsibble <- dom_ex_tp %>%
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(Date)) %>%
  as_tsibble(index = `Month`)

re_ex_tsibble <- re_ex_tp %>%
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(Date)) %>%
  as_tsibble(index = `Month`)
```

#### Convert to long format

```{r}
import_longer <- import_tsibble %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(target_countries),  
               names_to = "Country",
               values_to = "Trade_Value")

dom_ex_longer <- dom_ex_tsibble %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(target_countries),  
               names_to = "Country",
               values_to = "Trade_Value")

re_ex_longer <- re_ex_tsibble %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(target_countries),  
               names_to = "Country",
               values_to = "Trade_Value")
```

# V1: Total Merchandise Trade at Current Prices, 2020 - 2024

![Fig. 1](images/Screenshot%202025-03-09%20002743.png)

::: callout-note
## Comments on Fig. 1

#### **Pros:**

-   Provides an overview of Singapore's trade growth over time.

-   Clearly distinguishes between exports and imports with separate values.

-   Exports and imports are grouped together, making it easy to compare them by year.

#### **Cons:**

-   The visualization is heavily text-based, making it hard to grasp trends at a glance.

-   No clear graphical elements such as a trendline to show trends.

-   The numeric values can be overwhelming without visual cues.

-   No meaningful colour coding as every bar, be it import or export, is represented by a different colour.
:::

## Makeover

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(commodity_total, aes(x = Year, y = Total_Trade_Value / 1e6, color = `Data Series`, group = `Data Series`)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +  
  geom_point(size = 2) + 
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Total_Trade_Value / 1e6, 1)), 
            hjust = -0.2,  
            vjust = -0.5,  
            size = 2.5, color = "black") + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Yearly Trend of Merchandise Trade (2020-2024)",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Trade Value (S$ Billion)",
       color = "Trade Type") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2020, 2024, 1), limits = c(2019.5, 2024.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1), limits = c(min(commodity_total$Total_Trade_Value / 1e6),   max(commodity_total$Total_Trade_Value / 1e6) * 1.1))
```

::: callout-note
## Improvements over Fig. 1

-   It is more intuitive to read a time series from left to right.

-   Line graphs allow us to clearly see the trend over the years.

-   Less wordy. Only the important figures are shown.
:::

# V2: Merchandise Trade Performance with Major Trading Partners (2024)

![Fig. 2](images/Screenshot%202025-03-09%20002700.png)

::: callout-note
## Comments on Fig. 2

#### **Pros:**

-   The bubble chart format can convey a great deal of information within a small space. We can see Singapore's trade volume with many countries and whether Singapore has a positive net export or import with these countries.

-   Differentiates between import and export dominance via color coding.

-   We can immediately see who Singapore's biggest trading partners are based on the size of the bubble.

#### **Cons:**

-   A lot of numbers are presented, which might make it hard to compare at a glance.

-   No way to tell what the import and export trade values are. Can only see total trade value.

-   Can be hard to tell if a country is import or export dominant with Singapore if the centre of the bubble lies close to the dividing line (eg. Malaysia).
:::

## Makeover

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
p1 <- ggplot(annual_trade, aes(x = `Data Series`, y = Trade_Value/1e3, fill = Trade_Type)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") + 
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Trade_Value/1e3, 1)),  
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),  
            color = "black",  
            size = 3) +  
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Singapore's Total Merchandise Trade (2024)",
       x = "",
       y = "Total Trade Value (S$ Billion)",
       fill = "Trade Type") +
  coord_flip()

ggplotly(p1, tooltip = "text") 
```

::: callout-note
## Improvements on Fig. 2

-   Able to see detailed figures for imports and exports.

-   Can see which country has a trade surplus/deficit with Singapore at a glance.

-   Interactive - Able to isolate imports and exports for better comparison between countries.
:::

# V3: Non-Oil Merchandise Trade by Major Commodity Sections, 2024

![Fig. 3](images/Screenshot%202025-03-09%20121622.png)

::: callout-note
## Comments on Fig. 3

#### **Pros:**

-   Able to easily compare imports and exports within a commodity section

-   Colour coding for imports and exports

-   Category names are accompanied by graphics, making it visually appealing

#### **Cons:**

-   When a bar exceeds 60 Billion, it is represented by a segmented bar as can be seen on Machinery and Transport Equipment.

-   There is no indication on what amount each segment represents.

-   It is hard to count how many segments there are in the segmented bars.

-   The graphics can be distracting when trying to process the important numbers.
:::

## Makeover

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
commodity_category <- commodity_category %>%
  group_by(Trade_Type) %>%
  mutate(Percentage = (Total_Trade_Value / sum(Total_Trade_Value)) * 100)

# Create bar chart with percentage labels
ggplot(commodity_category, aes(x = Commodity, y = Total_Trade_Value/1e6, fill = Trade_Type)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +  
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(Total_Trade_Value/1e6, 1), " (", round(Percentage, 1), "%)")),  
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),  
            hjust = -0.3,  
            size = 2.5, color = "black") +  
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Non-Oil Merchandise Trade by Major Commodity Sections (2024)",
       x = "",
       y = "Total Trade Value (S$ Billion)",
       fill = "Trade Type") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, limits = c(0, max(commodity_category$Total_Trade_Value/1e6) * 1.2)) +  
  coord_flip()
```

::: callout-note
## Improvements on Fig. 3

-   Easier to compare between bars as they are not segmented.
-   Less fluff. Only the important numbers are shown.
:::

## Analysing the Time Series

```{r}
import_longer %>%

  gg_season(Trade_Value) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank()
  )
```

## Comments on the visual and analytical results

-   There was a sharp increase in exports, both domestic exports and re-exports, around 2020 to our ASEAN neighbours (Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand).

-   There has been an upward trend in imports in the last 5 years, particularly from Taiwan, the United States and Europe. Exports have been comparatively volatile.

-   There were no seasonal patterns observed in any of the data. This is because we are looking at trade volume as a whole. Individual commodity sections may reveal seasonal patterns particularly with food products.

-   Our top 5 trading partners are China, Europe, Malaysia, United States and Taiwan in that order.
